newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Donors ask Bangladesh to speed up reforms.
newsitem.headline: Donors ask Bangladesh to speed up reforms.

text.p: Bangladesh's overseas aid donors have asked the country's government to speed up economic reforms which they felt had been moving at snail's pace so far.
The donors' view was forwarded to the government at a meeting with finance ministry officials on Tuesday, an official with the World Bank mission in Dhaka said.
"Bangladesh must rush on reforms because it needs to reap the fruits soon. The process has been slow thus far," the official told Reuters on Thursday.

Donor countries and agencies provide Bangladesh with around $2 billion annually to finance development and imports, but they have warned that the funds could be shrinking in view of changing global requirements for aid.
Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria told Tuesday's meeting that his government was committed to carry out reforms as fast as possible.
Keeping that in view, Kibria said the government recently appointed new chiefs for the administrative reforms commission and the privatisation board, and set up a law reform commission.
"The government is finalising the process for holding election to the village councils by September next," the minister said.
Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina said before her election in June 1996 that if voted to power she would restructure and reinforce local administration in the country's 80,000-odd villages.

Tuesday's meeting was attended by representatives of the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, International Monetary Fund, USAID, UNDP, Britain, Japan, USA, Canada, France, Germany and the European Commission.
The donors criticised Bangladesh for its bloated government and asked for it to be trimmed, meeting sources said.
The size of the government has nearly doubled since 1971 while the number of ministries increased from 21 to 35 over the past 20 years, the donors quoted a 1997 World Bank report as saying.
The report said public sector employment increased from 450,000 in 1971 to nearly one million in 1992. Population grew at 2.5 percent a year over the period.
Inefficient public enterprises had caused Bangladesh to
lose nearly $1.86 billion between fiscal 1991/92 and 1995/96, Kazi Zafarullah, head of the Privatisation Board, said recently.
The board has listed 95 state-owned enterprises (SOEs) in jute, textile, engineering, sugar, food and chemicals sectors to be disposed of, Kibria told the donors.
The government had provided 420 billion taka ($9.76 billion) in subsidies to the SOEs over the past 21 years, finance ministry officials said.
The World Bank sources said that 225 non-financial SOEs under 39 corporations each year incurred losses equivalent to 27 percent of the fund for Bangladesh's annual development progarammes.
